How the estimates are made, and how wrong they are

  • Each measured chip and workload becomes one log-efficiency value. The model is log efficiency = workload level + a tier-by-workload shift + a generation effect + a tier effect + a chip-specific term, with ridge priors that shrink the shifts and the chip term toward zero. A chip with no measurements at all, such as the M1, M2 and M5 Ultra, gets only its generation and tier effects.
  • Throughput is fitted the same way. Published scores replace the model where they exist without matching power: the M3 Ultra scores 3,028 to 3,082 in Cinebench 2024 multi-core across reviews, and the M2 Ultra scores 28,550 in Cinebench R23.
  • Leave-one-out validation removes each measured cell in turn, refits, and predicts it. The root-mean-square error of those predictions is the uncertainty shown on every estimate: . Chips with no measurements get 1.5 times that.
  • Apple publishes idle and maximum wall power for each Mac mini and Mac Studio. Maximum power gives a hard floor, work per joule ≥ throughput ÷ maximum power, which clips the lower error bar of some desktop estimates. GPU estimates are not clipped, because Apple's maximum includes CPU and GPU together.
  • Apple's published power figures, shown in each point's details: for a Mac mini or Mac Studio, idle and maximum wall power from Apple's support pages (a CPU-only maximum for the M1, M2 and M2 Pro Mac mini); for a laptop, idle with the display on, sleep and off from its Product Environmental Report (115 V column), with the adapter and battery from the tech specs. The two idles are different tests (7 W against 3.96 W for the M2 Mac mini), so they are labelled apart; shared, repeated and stand-in tables are noted on each point. None is a measurement under the benchmark load. Only the desktop maximum bounds anything: a laptop can draw from its battery beyond its adapter, so the adapter is not used.
  • Power modes: Digital Trends measured the M4 Pro Mac mini in Low Power, Automatic and High Power mode (Cinebench 2024 multi-core 765, 1,622 and 1,707). Nobody published wall power per mode, so it is estimated from package power: about 46 W in High Power and 40 W in Automatic (Notebookcheck), and a 13.5 W cap in Low Power (Eclectic Light), times 1.15 for conversion losses plus 6 to 10 W for the rest of the machine.

What is missing and what was left out
  • Ultra chips under Cinebench. Reviews in English, German and Japanese give M3 Ultra scores but no wall power for the run. PC Watch reports about 146 W with Cinebench and a game running together. The M3 Ultra is measured only under HPL and LLM generation, where Jeff Geerling metered it at the wall. Its Cinebench points are estimates.
  • Other languages. Notebookcheck's German pages carry the same measurements as the English ones. Geekerwan (Chinese) publishes per-core power curves from package power, not wall power, and in video only. ITmedia and PC Watch (Japanese) give scores without matched wall power. Macwelt (German) gives about 124 W for the M4 Max Mac Studio under combined CPU and GPU load, which is not a single workload.
  • Blender. Render speeds are Blender Open Data medians (Blender 4.5), which pool every machine with a given chip, so a laptop, a Mac mini and a Mac Studio count alike. No source pairs them with metered wall energy, so all Blender points have estimated power: on the CPU, the same machine's Cinebench all-core wall power (0.9 to 1.1 times); on the GPU, 0.45 to 0.95 times its Cyberpunk 2077 wall power, a factor anchored only by one package-power reading. Error bars combine the spread of the median, the power range and the factor in quadrature on a log scale, and are about one standard deviation. The per-scene medians (monster, junkshop, classroom) come from the full Open Data snapshot and reuse the three-scene power. GPU points use each chip's full-core GPU; the cut-down variants in Open Data (for example the 30-core M3 Max or the 16-core M4 Pro) are left out, because no machine with them has a measured or modelled power on this page. Medians over three runs or fewer (M5 Ultra, M6, M5 Pro GPU) are marked as weaker measurements. Arm comparison chips: the Snapdragon X Elite has one Open Data run (Windows on Arm), shown as the three-scene sum and per scene; its Adreno GPU has no point because Cycles has no Adreno backend. Ampere has none: Open Data has no Linux-on-Arm launcher, and the Ampere Blender runs found elsewhere are fixed-sample render times without wall power, which do not convert to samples per minute. The NVIDIA N1X (CPU and GPU) and the Core 5 320 (CPU and its Intel Graphics) have Open Data runs only in Blender 5.2 or 5.3, which run up to 14% (CPU) and 13 to 28% (OptiX) faster than 4.5 on chips with both, so those points are marked as weaker with a wider speed range. Four GPU cells stay empty: the GB10 has no GPU run in Open Data, the i9-9880H MacBook Pro's Radeon Pro 5500M has Metal runs only up to Blender 4.2 and no wall reading under a GPU load, and the Intel Graphics of the Core Ultra 7 265K and Core Ultra 9 275HX have runs but no machine here with a wall reading of that iGPU at work (those machines render on their RTX cards, shown in the RTX rows).
  • Other games. Nobody publishes wall power for Baldur's Gate 3 or Assassin's Creed Shadows on these Macs, so those points borrow the Cyberpunk 2077 reading of the same machine. Total War: Pharaoh is left out because it is engine-limited near 50 to 56 fps from the M4 Pro up to the M5 Max, so it says little about the GPU; Shadow of the Tomb Raider because it has no M5, M5 Pro or M5 Max results. Upscaled or frame-generated results (MetalFX) and Geekerwan's figures, which are chip power rather than wall power, are not mixed in.
  • Comparison machines. Twenty-two Intel, AMD, Qualcomm and NVIDIA machines with wall readings, chosen for coverage: Notebookcheck's Cinebench and Cyberpunk 2077 wall readings, KitGuru's whole-PC reading for an RTX 4060 desktop, and Jeff Geerling's HPL and LLM runs, plus speed-only DGX Spark runs with estimated power. Card-only (board) power is never used, because every other point is the whole machine at the wall. In the matrix, n/a marks a cell that cannot exist (a CPU benchmark on a graphics card, Cinebench or Cyberpunk on the Linux-only GB10, a Blender GPU render on Qualcomm's Adreno) and – a cell nobody has measured. Where a review published no Cinebench 2024 power, another test's wall power stands in and the point is marked as weaker; some Cyberpunk frame rates come from the review rather than the efficiency chart used for the Macs, which reads 5 to 15% higher; the Snapdragon runs the game under emulation; discrete-GPU laptops and desktops are measured as a whole. Power modes matter more on these chips than on a Mac (an HX 370 laptop goes from 10.2 to 21.3 points per watt between 80 W and 15 W), and only one setting per machine is shown. None of these machines ran the Llama 2 7B Q4_0 all-chip test with a power meter. Eleven of the chips have that test (llama-bench tg128) from llama.cpp's CUDA, Vulkan and SYCL scoreboards and other public runs, on the backend a user of the machine would pick (CUDA on NVIDIA cards, Vulkan, ROCm or SYCL on AMD and Intel integrated GPUs, the CPU on the Snapdragon, which is faster there than its Adreno GPU), with wall power borrowed from the same machine on this page: 0.75 to 1.05 times Geerling's peak LLM reading where one exists, else 0.75 to 1.1 times its Cyberpunk 2077 wall power as for the Macs (0.6 to 1.0 times its Cinebench power for the Snapdragon's CPU run), widened because the speed comes from another machine; each point's note names the backend. The 155H, 265K, 275HX, Core 5 320, desktop RTX 4060 and N1X have no such run, so their LLM cells stay empty; the 265K and 275HX machines run LLMs on their RTX cards, which have their own rows.
  • Server CPUs. AMD EPYC, Intel Xeon, NVIDIA Grace and Ampere servers (Machine: Server, a hexagon) appear where their power can be cited: SPECpower_ssj2008 results (AC wall power, a server-only entry of the CPU all-cores Benchmark menu), Jeff Geerling's HPL runs on Ampere machines and his AmpereOne DeepSeek R1 671B run (wall), CPU-only TOP500/Green500 systems on the Linear algebra tab (per-node shares of system power, hollow and ringed as an indirect bound), and Blender Open Data medians with power borrowed from SPECpower. They are kept out of the matrix and All workloads. Left out: AWS Graviton (cloud instances expose no wall power), Grace HPL (no power for any CPU-only run), every GH200 and GB200 entry (the GPU is included), Fujitsu's A64FX (no vendor tier here), Cinebench and Geekbench on servers and workstations (none found with wall power), AmpereOne LLM runs other than DeepSeek R1 671B (no power), Blender medians with no SPECpower result for the same chip and socket count, and Threadripper and Xeon W workstations (no wall power). Arm servers have no Blender entries because the benchmark launcher has no Linux-on-Arm build.
  • M5 Ultra. The only wall-power figures found came from a blog whose 70B token rates are about 1.5 times the memory-bandwidth limit, so they are excluded. Its points here are model estimates.
  • iMacs are excluded because their wall power includes the built-in display.
  • Hollow points were measured with Cinebench R23 and converted to Cinebench 2024 units through the M4 Mac mini, which was measured in both. Five machines scored in both put the conversion error at about % for all-core and % for single-thread work.
  • Error bars on measured points span the 1st percentile to the maximum of instantaneous wall power during the run, so they overstate the uncertainty of the average.
